title: What's Good for Performance Often Isn't Good for Learning snt-good-for-learning/
author: Paul Kirschner
summary: In a prelude to a forthcoming book on instructional paradoxes, Paul Kirschner draws a sharp distinction between performance -- a short-term, fragile change in knowledge visible during or just after instruction -- and learning, a stable, enduring change in long-term memory. Citing Soderstrom and Bjork's definition, he explains that performance requires minimal, shallow cognitive processing and is fragmentary and easy to measure with a quick end-of-unit test, while learning requires deep processing (elaboration, organisation, critical thinking), is cumulative, and is genuinely hard to measure without delay and combination with other assessments. He illustrates the durability of true learning with a personal story about his senile grandfather, who could not consciously recall his childhood Russian but could still sing Russian nursery rhymes -- evidence the knowledge was never truly lost, just inaccessible. Kirschner is careful not to dismiss performance as worthless, but insists teachers must not confuse it with learning, and points to desirable difficulties and generative learning strategies as the two main evidence-based tool sets for producing real, durable learning rather than just short-term performance.
points: Kirschner's performance/learning distinction gives teachers a precise vocabulary for a problem they already sense intuitively: students who seem to 'get it' in the moment often can't recall the material weeks later.

The claim that performance is 'easy to see and measure' while learning is not explains why schools systematically over-rely on end-of-unit tests -- they measure the thing that's convenient to measure, not the thing that actually matters.

The grandfather anecdote is a vivid, memorable illustration of the relearning-is-faster-than-first-learning principle: forgotten material that was genuinely learned (not just performed) can resurface or be relearned far faster than acquiring it fresh.

By naming desirable difficulties and generative learning strategies as the two concrete tool sets for producing real learning, Kirschner links an abstract theoretical distinction directly back to established, actionable instructional research.
quotes: What we teach may go into our students' memory. During or directly after instruction they may be able to discuss ideas with classmates, answer questions, and even do their homework. But it isn't learning if nothing is retained.

Performance is a short-term change in one's knowledge or as Soderstrom and Bjork say, "temporary fluctuations in behavior or knowledge that can be observed and measured during or immediately after the acquisition process".
Grandpa Jack couldn’t remember the rhymes but they were still there in his long-term memory. He hadn’t forgotten them.

Performance requires very little cognitive processing and this processing also is shallow while learning, on the other hand, involves deep processing activities like elaboration, organisation, and critical thinking.
Finally, and this is probably the biggest problem with teaching for learning, is that performance is easy to see and measure while learning isn't.
You want that what you’ve taught to be remembered, retrieved when needed, and applied in both familiar and new situations (transfer).
